h: Mushrooms, an organ and the Last Night
p: Look up during a show and you'll spot the hall's famous 'mushrooms', the big fibreglass discs hanging from the ceiling. They were installed in the late 1960s to tame the echo that had dogged the hall since it opened, and they've become part of its character. Behind the stage, the mighty Grand Organ, with thousands of pipes, is a sight in its own right, and it's thrilling to hear it at full blast.

Outside, take a walk right round the building. A mosaic frieze runs around the top, showing the triumph of arts and sciences, a nod to Prince Albert's dream of a cultural quarter in South Kensington. The hall was built in his memory after his death, and the area around it, with its colleges and museums, was all part of that grand vision.

The Last Night of the Proms each September is a famous, flag-waving British institution, but don't overlook the rest of the season. One of the joys of the Proms is that you can stand in the Arena or Gallery with a low-cost day ticket, which makes it a brilliant way to try classical music without a big commitment. Bring patience, as there can be queues.

Before or after a performance, the area has plenty to fill an afternoon. Kensington Gardens are just across the road, with the Serpentine galleries a short walk into the park, and the Royal College of Music is round the back. Arrive with time to spare, since finding your door and your seat in a building this size can take longer than you think.
